source: These pathways are consistent with well-characterized aspects of the early host response to malaria, in which parasites are sensed by pattern recognition receptors, promoting the production of cytokines (Gowda and Wu, 2018), and ensuing mobilization of early myeloid progenitors from bone marrow to establish emergency myelopoiesis in the spleen (Nahrendorf et al., 2021; Belyaev et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a well-characterized aspect of the host response, supported by citations.

claim: Proinflammatory and immunoregulatory cytokines play important roles in shaping T-cell activation and adaptive immune responses.
source: Proinflammatory and immunoregulatory cytokines play important roles in shaping T-cell activation and adaptive immune responses (Urban et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: Reactive oxygen species produced by phagocytic cells in response to parasites contribute to inflammation and tissue damage.
source: Reactive oxygen species produced by phagocytic cells in response to parasites, and through cell-free heme released during hemolysis, contribute to inflammation and tissue damage (Vasquez et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: Reactive oxygen species produced through cell-free heme released during hemolysis contribute to inflammation and tissue damage.
source: Reactive oxygen species produced by phagocytic cells in response to parasites, and through cell-free heme released during hemolysis, contribute to inflammation and tissue damage (Vasquez et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: The top GO terms for PC1 in the Milne et al. CHMI data set were related to bacterial and interferon-γ responses.
source: In the Milne et al. CHMI data set, the top GO terms for PC1 were related to bacterial and interferon-γ responses, whilst PC2 was related to viral and interferon-γ responses (Supplementary file 11).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene ontology analysis conducted in this study.

claim: The top GO terms for PC2 in the Milne et al. CHMI data set were related to viral and interferon-γ responses.
source: In the Milne et al. CHMI data set, the top GO terms for PC1 were related to bacterial and interferon-γ responses, whilst PC2 was related to viral and interferon-γ responses (Supplementary file 11).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene ontology analysis conducted in this study.

claim: Timing and duration of IFN-γ production are important determinants of whether its effects are protective or pathogenic.
source: These again are consistent with the earliest innate responses to malaria parasites, with timing and duration of IFN-γ production being important determinants of whether its effects are protective or pathogenic (King et al., 2015; Walther et al., 2009; Hermsen et al., 2003; De Souza et al., 1997; Mitchell et al., 2005; Amani et al., 2000; Villegas-Mendez et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The direction of changes in gene expression in the mouse models were less concordant with those in human severe malaria phenotypes than observed in comparisons with uncomplicated malaria.
source: Overall, the direction of changes in gene expression in the mouse models were less concordant with those in human SM phenotypes than we observed in the comparisons with UM (Supplementary file 9, Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative transcriptomic analysis conducted in this study.

claim: There was much clearer variation between the different mouse models in how closely the changes in expression of individual genes recapitulated those observed in each human severe malaria manifestation.
source: There was, however, much clearer variation between the different mouse models in how closely the changes in expression of individual genes recapitulated those observed in each human SM manifestation (Figure 3b, d and f).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative transcriptomic analysis conducted in this study.

claim: Hyperlactatemia is a relatively common manifestation of severe malaria in children.
source: Hyperlactatemia is a relatively common manifestation of SM in children, and an independent predictor of death (Krishna et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: Hyperlactatemia is an independent predictor of death in severe malaria.
source: Hyperlactatemia is a relatively common manifestation of SM in children, and an independent predictor of death (Krishna et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: P. yoelii 17XL and P. berghei NK65 models most closely recapitulated the changes in gene expression associated with hyperlactatemia in Gambian children.
source: PCA revealed that P. yoelii 17XL and P. berghei NK65 models most closely recapitulated the changes in gene expression associated with this disease phenotype in Gambian children (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a finding from the PCA analysis conducted in this study.

claim: Neutrophil degranulation was identified as driving PC1 in the comparison with human hyperlactatemia.
source: We performed GO enrichment analysis on the genes contributing most to the principal components explaining the greatest proportion of variation between the mouse models and human disease, identifying neutrophil degranulation driving PC1 and myeloid leukocyte activation driving PC2 (Supplementary file 11).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene ontology analysis conducted in this study.

claim: Myeloid leukocyte activation was identified as driving PC2 in the comparison with human hyperlactatemia.
source: We performed GO enrichment analysis on the genes contributing most to the principal components explaining the greatest proportion of variation between the mouse models and human disease, identifying neutrophil degranulation driving PC1 and myeloid leukocyte activation driving PC2 (Supplementary file 11).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene ontology analysis conducted in this study.

claim: P. yoelii 17XL was the mouse model with greatest similarity in gene expression changes to human cerebral malaria.
source: In the comparison of the mouse models with the human CM phenotype (Figure 3d), P. yoelii 17XL was again the mouse model with greatest similarity in gene expression changes, and GO analysis revealed that myeloid leucocyte activation and neutrophil degranulation were again the most enriched GO terms amongst the genes explaining the greatest variation between models (Supplementary file 11).
evidence: This is a finding from the PCA analysis conducted in this study.

claim: Myeloid leucocyte activation and neutrophil degranulation were the most enriched GO terms amongst the genes explaining the greatest variation between models in the comparison with human cerebral malaria.
source: In the comparison of the mouse models with the human CM phenotype (Figure 3d), P. yoelii 17XL was again the mouse model with greatest similarity in gene expression changes, and GO analysis revealed that myeloid leucocyte activation and neutrophil degranulation were again the most enriched GO terms amongst the genes explaining the greatest variation between models (Supplementary file 11).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene ontology analysis conducted in this study.

claim: P. yoelii 17XL was placed closest to human cerebral malaria plus hyperlactatemia in the PCA plot.
source: Findings were similar when we compared the changes in gene expression in the mouse models with those in children with UM versus children with the most severe phenotype where both CM and HL are present (CH) (Lee et al., 2018b). P. yoelii 17XL was placed closest to human CH in the PCA plot (Figure 3g), and the genes contributing most to PC1 and PC2 were again enriched in neutrophil degranulation and myeloid leukocyte activation GO terms (Supplementary file 11).
evidence: This is a finding from the PCA analysis conducted in this study.

claim: The genes contributing most to PC1 and PC2 in the comparison with human cerebral malaria plus hyperlactatemia were enriched in neutrophil degranulation and myeloid leukocyte activation GO terms.
source: Findings were similar when we compared the changes in gene expression in the mouse models with those in children with UM versus children with the most severe phenotype where both CM and HL are present (CH) (Lee et al., 2018b). P. yoelii 17XL was placed closest to human CH in the PCA plot (Figure 3g), and the genes contributing most to PC1 and PC2 were again enriched in neutrophil degranulation and myeloid leukocyte activation GO terms (Supplementary file 11).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene ontology analysis conducted in this study.

claim: Different aspects of neutrophil function could contribute to pathogenesis or protection from severe malaria in both humans and some mouse models.
source: The finding that neutrophil degranulation and myeloid leukocyte activation pathway genes account for the greatest variation between human SM phenotypes and the mouse models is consistent with increasing evidence that different aspects of neutrophil function could contribute to pathogenesis or protection from SM in both humans and some mouse models (Lee et al., 2018b; Knackstedt et al., 2019; Georgiadou et al., 2021; Aitken et al., 2018; Feintuch et al., 2016; Sercundes et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as consistent with increasing evidence, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The relative frequency of different manifestations of P. falciparum severe malaria varies across different geographic locations.
source: The relative frequency of different manifestations of P. falciparum SM varies across different geographic locations, influenced by the intensity of exposure to malaria, naturally acquired immunity, and age of individuals (Wassmer et al., 2015; Okiro et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: The relative frequency of different manifestations of P. falciparum severe malaria is influenced by the intensity of exposure to malaria.
source: The relative frequency of different manifestations of P. falciparum SM varies across different geographic locations, influenced by the intensity of exposure to malaria, naturally acquired immunity, and age of individuals (Wassmer et al., 2015; Okiro et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: The relative frequency of different manifestations of P. falciparum severe malaria is influenced by naturally acquired immunity.
source: The relative frequency of different manifestations of P. falciparum SM varies across different geographic locations, influenced by the intensity of exposure to malaria, naturally acquired immunity, and age of individuals (Wassmer et al., 2015; Okiro et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: The relative frequency of different manifestations of P. falciparum severe malaria is influenced by age of individuals.
source: The relative frequency of different manifestations of P. falciparum SM varies across different geographic locations, influenced by the intensity of exposure to malaria, naturally acquired immunity, and age of individuals (Wassmer et al., 2015; Okiro et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Changes in gene expression associated with the same disease manifestation may vary between studies in different populations.
source: Changes in gene expression associated with the same disease manifestation may also vary between studies in different populations, under genetic and environmental influences, and due to technical differences in the methods used to assess gene expression (Driss et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as a known source of variation, supported by citations.

claim: There was relatively high (78%) concordance of differentially expressed genes in the Gambian cerebral malaria plus hyperlactatemia versus uncomplicated malaria and Gabonese cerebral malaria/cerebral malaria plus hyperlactatemia versus uncomplicated malaria comparisons.
source: Nevertheless, there was relatively high (78%) concordance of differentially expressed genes in the Gambian CH-UM and Gabonese CM/CH-UM comparisons (Supplementary files 1D and 9).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative analysis conducted in this study.

claim: P. yoelii 17XL most closely recapitulated the differential expression seen in Gabonese children with cerebral malaria/cerebral malaria plus hyperlactatemia versus uncomplicated malaria.
source: Comparison of changes in gene expression between early and late stages of the mouse infections with those between Gabonese children with UM and CM/CH revealed that P. yoelii 17XL most closely recapitulated the differential expression seen in humans (Figure 4, Supplementary files 12 and 7).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative transcriptomic analysis conducted in this study.

claim: The innate immune response and leukocyte mediated immunity were the main drivers of variation between models in the comparison with Gabonese children.
source: GO analysis confirmed that the innate immune response and leukocyte mediated immunity were the main drivers of variation between models, similar to the analysis in Gambian children (Supplementary file 11).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene ontology analysis conducted in this study.

claim: The selection of the most appropriate mouse model for investigation of a particular mechanism of interest should not be made solely on the similarity of clinical phenotype in humans and mice.
source: An important implication of our findings is that the selection of the most appropriate mouse model for investigation of a particular mechanism of interest should not be made solely on the similarity of clinical phenotype in humans and mice.
evidence: This is stated as an implication of the study's findings.

claim: The selection of the most appropriate mouse model should be based on the degree of concordance of expression of genes associated with the mechanism of interest.
source: We propose that it should also be based on the degree of concordance of expression of genes associated with the mechanism of interest.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the study's findings.

claim: Failure to consider the similarities and differences in biological processes indicated by gene expression could lead to experiments targeting pathways that are not involved in the host response to a particular mouse malaria parasite.
source: Failure to consider the similarities and differences in biological processes indicated by gene expression could lead to experiments targeting pathways that are not involved in the host response to a particular mouse malaria parasite, making the experiments futile, unethical, and potentially leading to erroneous conclusions.
evidence: This is stated as a potential consequence of not considering gene expression concordance.

claim: P. yoelii 17XL infected mice develop extreme hyperlactatemia at levels similar to those seen in human hyperlactatemia and cerebral malaria plus hyperlactatemia.
source: This mouse model not only develops a very high parasite load, but our data suggest lethality at 5–7 days post-infection is part of a multisystem disorder, accompanied by extreme hyperlactatemia at levels similar to those seen in human HL and CH.
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments conducted in this study.

claim: Lethality at 5–7 days post-infection in P. yoelii 17XL is part of a multisystem disorder.
source: This mouse model not only develops a very high parasite load, but our data suggest lethality at 5–7 days post-infection is part of a multisystem disorder, accompanied by extreme hyperlactatemia at levels similar to those seen in human HL and CH.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data from the experiments conducted in this study.

claim: The lack of a rodent model to study malaria-induced hyperlactatemia has held back understanding of the mechanisms causing such high levels of lactate.
source: Until now, the lack of a rodent model to study malaria-induced hyperlactatemia has held back understanding of the mechanisms causing such high levels of lactate and how these relate to the increased risk of death in patients with malaria.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation in the field prior to this study.

claim: P. yoelii 17XL infection of C57BL/6J mice is an attractive model for further translational research on the severe malaria hyperlactatemia phenotype.
source: P. yoelii 17XL infection of C57BL/6J mice is an attractive model for further translational research on this SM phenotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: Extravascular fibrinogen leak was identified in the brains of P. yoelii 17XL infected mice.
source: In the brains of P. yoelii 17XL infected mice, we identified extravascular fibrinogen leak.
evidence: This is a finding from the histopathological analysis conducted in this study.

claim: P. yoelii 17XL infected mice may be in the process of developing a neurological syndrome at the time they reach the humane endpoint.
source: This suggests that these mice may be in the process of developing a neurological syndrome at the time they reach the humane endpoint and may explain why this model showed transcriptional similarity to human CM.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the histopathological findings.

claim: The transcriptional similarity of P. yoelii 17XL to the human severe anemia phenotype is consistent with the severe anemia and high parasite load which occurs in this infection.
source: The transcriptional similarity of Py17XL to the human SA phenotype is consistent with the SA and high parasite load which occurs in this infection.
evidence: This is stated as a consistency between transcriptional and clinical findings.

claim: The maximum parasitemia (~80%) seen in P. yoelii 17XL infection is much higher than that typically seen in human severe malaria (~10%).
source: The maximum parasitemia (~80%) seen in Py17XL infection is much higher than that typically seen in human SM (~10%) (Cunnington et al., 2013), although the sequestration of P. falciparum-infected red cells in human SM means that total parasite load may be several fold-higher than indicated by peripheral blood parasitemia (Cunnington et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison of observed parasitemia levels, supported by citation.

claim: The sequestration of P. falciparum-infected red cells in human severe malaria means that total parasite load may be several fold-higher than indicated by peripheral blood parasitemia.
source: The maximum parasitemia (~80%) seen in Py17XL infection is much higher than that typically seen in human SM (~10%) (Cunnington et al., 2013), although the sequestration of P. falciparum-infected red cells in human SM means that total parasite load may be several fold-higher than indicated by peripheral blood parasitemia (Cunnington et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of human severe malaria, supported by citation.

claim: A strength of analyzing the blood transcriptome is that it represents the systemic host response to infection.
source: A strength of analyzing the blood transcriptome is that it represents the systemic host response to infection, capturing both the direct influence of an infectious agent on blood leukocytes, and the response of blood leukocytes to mediators released into the circulation by cells in other organs.
evidence: This is stated as a strength of the methodology used in the study.

claim: The blood transcriptome captures both the direct influence of an infectious agent on blood leukocytes, and the response of blood leukocytes to mediators released into the circulation by cells in other organs.
source: A strength of analyzing the blood transcriptome is that it represents the systemic host response to infection, capturing both the direct influence of an infectious agent on blood leukocytes, and the response of blood leukocytes to mediators released into the circulation by cells in other organs.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of blood transcriptome analysis.

claim: The blood transcriptome cannot assess the concordance of processes occurring within specific organs that do not produce changes in gene expression of circulating leukocytes.
source: However, the blood transcriptome cannot assess the concordance of processes occurring within specific organs that do not produce changes in gene expression of circulating leukocytes, and our data should not be used to prevent testing of reasonable hypotheses about such tissue-specific interactions.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the methodology used in the study.

claim: The findings were broadly consistent when comparisons were performed across independent studies conducted in different locations and using different transcriptomic methods.
source: Reassuringly, our findings were broadly consistent when we performed comparisons across independent studies conducted in different locations and using different transcriptomic methods.
evidence: This is stated as a finding about the robustness of the results.

claim: P. yoelii 17XL and P. berghei NK65 infected mice developed dramatic hyperlactatemia at maximum severity with concentrations similar to the maximum values seen in human hyperlactatemia.
source: Small differences, if any, were noticed at the uncomplicated stage early in infection, while at maximum severity P. yoelii 17XL and P. berghei NK65 infected mice developed dramatic hyperlactatemia with concentrations similar to the maximum values seen in human HL (Lee et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is a finding from the lactate measurements conducted in this study, shown in Figure 5a.

claim: P. yoelii 17XL achieves much higher parasite load than other mouse models.
source: Human SA is often associated with very high parasite biomass (Cunnington et al., 2013) and P. yoelii 17XL achieves much higher parasite load than other mouse models (Figure 1) as well as causing rapid and profound anemia (Couper et al., 2007; Totino et al., 2010; Figure 5b).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study, shown in Figure 1.

claim: P. yoelii 17XL causes rapid and profound anemia.
source: Human SA is often associated with very high parasite biomass (Cunnington et al., 2013) and P. yoelii 17XL achieves much higher parasite load than other mouse models (Figure 1) as well as causing rapid and profound anemia (Couper et al., 2007; Totino et al., 2010; Figure 5b).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study, supported by citations and shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Human severe anemia is often associated with very high parasite biomass.
source: Human SA is often associated with very high parasite biomass (Cunnington et al., 2013) and P. yoelii 17XL achieves much higher parasite load than other mouse models (Figure 1) as well as causing rapid and profound anemia (Couper et al., 2007; Totino et al., 2010; Figure 5b).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: P. yoelii 17XL was originally described as a virulent clone causing cerebral malaria-like pathology.
source: P. yoelii 17XL was originally described as a virulent clone causing CM-like pathology (Yoeli and Hargreaves, 1974), but it has subsequently been replaced by P. berghei ANKA as the most commonly used model of experimental CM.
evidence: This is stated as historical information, supported by citation.

claim: P. berghei ANKA has replaced P. yoelii 17XL as the most commonly used model of experimental cerebral malaria.
source: P. yoelii 17XL was originally described as a virulent clone causing CM-like pathology (Yoeli and Hargreaves, 1974), but it has subsequently been replaced by P. berghei ANKA as the most commonly used model of experimental CM.
evidence: This is stated as a change in common practice in the field.

claim: One of the key pathological mechanisms leading to death in pediatric cerebral malaria is brain swelling due to extravascular fluid leak.
source: Since one of the key pathological mechanisms leading to death in pediatric CM is brain swelling due to extravascular fluid leak (Moxon et al., 2020), we examined the presence of extravascular fibrinogen (Georgiadou et al., 2021) as an indicator of vascular leak in the brains of both P. berghei ANKA and P. yoelii 17XL infected mice compared to uninfected mice (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: Brains from both P. berghei ANKA and P. yoelii 17XL infections had areas that stained positively for perivascular fibrinogen.
source: We found that brains from both infections had areas that stained positively for perivascular fibrinogen (indicative of vascular leak), while additionally some of the vessels from P. yoelii 17XL infected mice showed strong intravascular staining, suggestive of microthrombus formation (Figure 5c, iv ), another mechanism that has been implicated in human CM (Moxon et al., 2020; Georgiadou et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from the histopathological analysis conducted in this study, shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Some vessels from P. yoelii 17XL infected mice showed strong intravascular staining, suggestive of microthrombus formation.
source: We found that brains from both infections had areas that stained positively for perivascular fibrinogen (indicative of vascular leak), while additionally some of the vessels from P. yoelii 17XL infected mice showed strong intravascular staining, suggestive of microthrombus formation (Figure 5c, iv ), another mechanism that has been implicated in human CM (Moxon et al., 2020; Georgiadou et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from the histopathological analysis conducted in this study, shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Microthrombus formation is a mechanism that has been implicated in human cerebral malaria.
source: We found that brains from both infections had areas that stained positively for perivascular fibrinogen (indicative of vascular leak), while additionally some of the vessels from P. yoelii 17XL infected mice showed strong intravascular staining, suggestive of microthrombus formation (Figure 5c, iv ), another mechanism that has been implicated in human CM (Moxon et al., 2020; Georgiadou et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.
